logline: In 22nd-century Japan, the authoritarian Sibyl System measures citizens' psychological states to predict crime - but rookie Inspector Akane Tsunemori begins to question whether a society policed by probability can ever be just.

renewal.note: The original three-season run concluded in 2019. A film trilogy and compilation films followed, with Providence (2023) serving as the franchise's current narrative endpoint.

bollymeter.basis: RT 87% from 3 critics and MAL 8.32 from over 830,000 users confirm Season 1 as a landmark cyberpunk thriller; praised for philosophical depth, Gen Urobuchi's writing, and Production I.G's atmospheric craft.

pull_quotes.text: With a thought-provoking narrative, fascinating characters and stunning animation, Psycho-Pass is a thrilling anime from start to finish.
Psycho-Pass excels in character depth, which reaches a level very uncommon among anime.

seasons.review_body: Season 1 aired on Fuji TV's Noitamina block from October 2012 to March 2013, with series composition by Gen Urobuchi (Fate/Zero, Puella Magi Madoka Magica) and animation by Production I.G. Critics at CBR and Asian Movie Pulse converged on the same virtues: the moral complexity of the Sibyl System as a critique of surveillance capitalism, the cat-and-mouse dynamic between Inspector Tsunemori and the criminally asymptomatic villain Makishima, and the dense Blade Runner-adjacent world-building delivered without exposition dumps. The MAL community rating of 8.32 from over 830,000 scorers places it among the decade's most influential cyberpunk anime. Where detractors push back - on internal logic and graphic violence - supporters counter that the bleakness is structural argument, not wallowing.

episode_reviews.title: Crime Coefficient
episode_reviews.review_body: Psycho-Pass Season 1 Episode 1 'Crime Coefficient' aired October 12, 2012 on Fuji TV's Noitamina block as the premiere of Gen Urobuchi and Production I.G's 22-episode cyberpunk thriller. MyAnimeList users scored the series 8.32 from over 830,000 ratings. CBR called it 'a thought-provoking narrative, fascinating characters and stunning animation from start to finish'; Asian Movie Pulse noted it 'excels in character depth, which reaches a level very uncommon among anime.' The premiere introduces the Sibyl System's logic with deliberate efficiency: a world where a psychometric number defines whether you live free or die is rendered through Akane Tsunemori's first field deployment alongside the Enforcers. The show does not ease into its moral question - the first deployment makes the stakes immediately visible. The dominator weapon that fires based on psychological readings rather than criminal action is the premiere's central formal object, and the first time it targets a victim the system's terrifying neutrality is made concrete.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere introduces the Sibyl System's logic with deliberate efficiency - a world where a number defines whether you live free or die. Akane Tsunemori's first field deployment alongside the Enforcers establishes the moral stakes instantly: justice administered by algorithm, and the humans trapped inside it.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The first time an Enforcer's dominator targets a victim and the numbers refuse to lie - the system's terrifying neutrality made visible.

episode_reviews.title: Saint's Devil
episode_reviews.review_body: Psycho-Pass Season 1 Episode 11 'Saint's Devil' aired December 14, 2012 on Fuji TV's Noitamina block as the mid-season pivot of Gen Urobuchi's 22-episode series. MAL users scored it 8.32 from over 830,000 ratings. CBR called the series 'a thought-provoking narrative with fascinating characters'; Asian Movie Pulse noted it 'excels in character depth at a level very uncommon among anime.' This episode fully reveals Shogo Makishima and reframes the entire premise of the series: he emerges not as a monster but as a philosophical argument against the Sibyl System, a living refutation of the assumption that psychological risk can be algorithmically detected. That reframing makes him more frightening than any conventional criminal. The moment Makishima acts without a flicker of Psycho-Pass elevation is the system's fundamental failure made immediate and human - the episode the fandom returns to when debating whether the series' central question has an answer.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The mid-season pivot that fully reveals the antagonist and reframes the entire premise. Makishima emerges not as a monster but as a philosophical argument against the Sibyl System - which makes him more frightening than any mere criminal. The episode the fandom returns to for debate.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Makishima acts without a flicker of Psycho-Pass elevation - the system's fundamental failure made human and immediate.

episode_reviews.title: Where the Thought Police Wait
episode_reviews.review_body: Psycho-Pass Season 1 Episode 22 'Where the Thought Police Wait' aired March 22, 2013 on Fuji TV's Noitamina block as the finale of Gen Urobuchi's 22-episode series. MAL users scored it 8.32 from over 830,000 ratings. CBR called it 'a thought-provoking narrative that remains compelling from start to finish'; Common Sense Media noted 'its ability to engage with complex moral questions in a nuanced way makes it compelling for those seeking mature content.' The finale delivers its moral verdict without softening it: Akane emerges carrying knowledge about the Sibyl System that the system would prefer buried, and she chooses to operate within it anyway. The ending is neither triumphant nor despairing but lucid - which the show frames as its own kind of bravery. The final confrontation between Akane's idealism and the pragmatic compromise she reaches is the season's intellectual closing argument, and Gen Urobuchi does not resolve it in favour of either position.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale delivers its moral verdict without softening it: Akane emerges from the season carrying knowledge the system would prefer buried, and chooses to operate within it anyway. The ending is neither triumphant nor despairing - it is lucid, which is its own kind of bravery.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Akane's final confrontation with what she now knows about Sibyl - the moment where idealism and pragmatism negotiate a truce.

critic_note.text: Its ability to engage with complex moral questions in a nuanced way makes it compelling for those seeking mature content.

bollymeter.basis: Audience reception dropped sharply without Urobuchi's writing; the compressed 11-episode structure and a less compelling antagonist could not replicate Season 1's philosophical weight.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 aired October to December 2014, produced without Gen Urobuchi and written by Tow Ubukata. The condensed 11-episode count and a new antagonist - Kirito Kamui, who can remain invisible to Sibyl - built an interesting concept but delivered it with less philosophical rigour than its predecessor. Audience scores on MAL dropped to the high 6s, and critical consensus noted the season leaned on action spectacle at the expense of the methodical moral inquiry that made Season 1 essential. Loyal to the franchise's world and visuals, but measurably diminished as a drama.
seasons.season_over_season: Loses Urobuchi's writing and the careful intellectual scaffolding of Season 1; faster, louder, and philosophically thinner despite a genuinely interesting central conceit.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 introduced a new duo of Inspectors and longer 45-minute episodes, recovering some critical respect with its expanded canvas and a politically ambitious storyline.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 debuted October 2019 with a restructured format: eight episodes of roughly 45 minutes each, effectively doubling the runtime per instalment. The new protagonist duo of Kei Mikhail Ignatov and Nobuchika Ginoza’s son Arata Shindo brings fresh perspectives to the franchise’s central question. The political scope widens to include immigration and stateless populations, with the worldbuilding standing as the most ambitious since Season 1. MAL scores stabilise in the low 7s, reflecting engagement with the new leads while also suggesting that the film-trilogy resolution, First Inspector (2020), is needed to complete the season’s narrative arc.
seasons.season_over_season: A genuine recovery from Season 2, with longer episodes and political ambition that recalls the franchise's best work - though it requires the follow-up film to fully resolve.
